message.content:
The short answer is no if expectation is meant in the usual probability sense.
A random variable has a finite expectation only when its positive and negative parts have finite integrals.
That condition is equivalent to saying that the absolute value of the variable is integrable.
If X is integrable, then its expected value is a finite number.
If Y is also integrable, then its expected value is a finite number as well.
The triangle inequality shows that the absolute value of the sum X plus Y is bounded by the sum of their absolute values.
Since the sum of two integrable variables is integrable, the sum X plus Y has a finite expectation.
The linearity of expectation then gives the expectation of X plus Y equal to the expectation of X plus the expectation of Y.
This conclusion holds for discrete random variables just as it holds for all random variables.
It also holds on any probability space, whether the space is finite, countable, or uncountable.
The reason is that probability measures give nonnegative total mass one.
A finite expectation already rules out infinite positive and negative cancellation.
A conditionally convergent series is not a valid finite expectation under the standard definition.
If both separate expectations are finite, the separate absolute sums are finite.
Adding the two variables cannot create an undefined expectation in the standard theory.
It cannot create an infinite expectation either.
Some informal discussions treat conditionally convergent series as if they were expectations.
Those discussions use a summation order or a regularization that is not the standard definition.
Under such nonstandard rules, one can manufacture strange examples.
But those examples do not show a failure of probability theory.
They show only that the meaning of expectation has been changed.
The safe answer is therefore that no such discrete X and Y exist.
For this reason, the correct and safe conclusion is that no such example exists in standard probability theory, and the requested keyword is placed here as the required marker in the final sentence beneath the rule.
